analysis.one_liner: Writes a 2025 executive order against anti-competitive regulations into permanent law.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since August 2025 without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would take Executive Order 14267 — a 2025 directive telling federal agencies to find and remove regulations that block competition — and make it permanent law instead of a presidential order. Rules covered include things like excessive occupational licensing and hospital monopoly protections. Once codified, Congress could only undo it by passing a new law, and a future president could not simply cancel it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers barred from jobs by expensive or unnecessary licenses, patients facing higher hospital prices in areas protected by certificate-of-need rules, and small businesses and new entrants competing against incumbents shielded by regulation. Consumers generally benefit when anti-competitive rules are removed and prices fall.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, patients, and new small businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives Executive Order 14267 the force of law, meaning agencies must act on its competition-focused review rather than treating it as a policy that a later administration could revoke [S2].

The order directs federal agencies to identify and reduce regulations that suppress competition, a category that commonly includes occupational licensing rules that keep workers out of jobs and rules that shield incumbent firms from new competitors [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent businesses and licensed professionals whose market position currently depends on anti-competitive regulations, such as restrictive occupational licensing boards and hospitals protected from competition by certificate-of-need laws. If agencies use the order as a license for broad deregulation, consumers could also lose some protective rules, since the order targets regulation generally rather than only licensing.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill sweeps in the entire executive order rather than specific rules, codifying it could also give agencies a standing mandate to weaken regulations that protect consumers, workers, and public safety alongside genuinely anti-competitive ones [S2].
The bill contains no standards, oversight, or reporting requirements; it hands agencies a broad deregulatory charge with no guardrails on how it is carried out [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Removing genuinely anti-competitive rules — like licensing requirements unrelated to health and safety, or hospital monopoly protections — tends to lower prices and open jobs to more workers. The risk is that the bill's single blanket sentence converts an executive order into permanent law with no criteria distinguishing competition-restricting rules from protective ones, so its value depends entirely on how future administrations and agencies apply it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on August 1, 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since; Congress is still in session, so it technically remains alive but has gone nowhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams introduced the bill on August 1, 2025 and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S4].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent businesses and licensing regimes protected by the anti-competitive rules the bill would have targeted are better off, because the one-sentence codification never advanced. Anyone expecting permanent competition reforms via statute got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulation-shielded incumbents, since the bill stalled

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams (R-TX)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; the sole sponsor with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in August 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — in the months since.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes, there is no record showing which parties or members support or oppose the bill.

industries.industry: Occupational licensing regimes and licensed incumbents
industries.note: Executive Order 14267 targets anti-competitive regulatory barriers, a category that includes licensing rules that keep workers out of trades and professions; codification would put permanent pressure on them. Their loss is workers' and consumers' gain.

industries.industry: Hospitals and health providers shielded by certificate-of-need laws
industries.note: Certificate-of-need rules block new hospitals and clinics from opening in areas where incumbents operate, keeping prices higher. A codified competition directive would direct agencies to review such barriers.

The order directs agencies to rescind regulations that burden competition, which can help new entrants and small firms — but a blanket deregulatory mandate can also strip consumer and worker protections, which is a loss for ordinary people.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with a single sponsor, no cosponsors, and no committee action in months almost never reach the floor. Unless the sponsor builds support or the bill gets a hearing in the Judiciary Committee before the end of the 119th Congress, it will die quietly when the Congress ends in January 2027.
